title: "Day 1 — The 7 Patterns of R (and Python's Zen)"
subtitle: "Week 1 · Why R feels chaotic, and the map that fixes it"
---

## Cheat sheet (30 seconds)

| # | R pattern | One-line recognition cue | Python counterpart |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vectorization | "no loop, whole vector at once" | numpy / pandas vectorization |
| 2 | The pipe `|>` | "data first, then verbs" | method chaining `.query().assign()` |
| 3 | df-in, df-out | "function eats data.frame, returns data.frame" | functions taking/returning DataFrames |
| 4 | Formula `y ~ x` | "tilde = model spec" | patsy/statsmodels `"mpg ~ am"` |
| 5 | Tidy eval `{{ var }}` | "column names as arguments" | — (plain string/kwargs) |
| 6 | Functionals `map()` | "loop hidden in a function" | comprehensions / `map()` |
| 7 | S3 dispatch | "`plot(x)` does different things per class" | `__repr__`, dunder dispatch |

## Why R feels "too flexible" (10 min)

Three design facts explain almost all of the chaos:

**1. R is two dialects welded together.** Base R carries its S-language
heritage: `sapply()`, `df$x[cond]`, `attach()`, partial matching, loops.
The tidyverse (2016–) rebuilt the common operations with consistent names,
data-first arguments, and strict checks. When AI generates code, it mixes the
dialects mid-script — `dplyr::filter` in one line, `df[df$x > 2,]` in the
next — and each dialect has *three* ways to do anything, so you see a new
style every time.

**2. R's superpowers are invisible.** Vectorization, formula syntax,
functional programming, and S3 dispatch are *why* idiomatic R looks nothing
like idiomatic Python or C. Nobody names them for you, so idiomatic R reads
as magic. Today we name them.

**3. R trusts you too much.** Silent coercion, partial argument matching,
growing vectors, `NA` propagation — R rarely stops you; it just does
*something*. Good R code is built from patterns that make the trusting parts
predictable.

> ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
> ## Rule 1 of this course
> **Write tidyverse-first.** Learn to *read* base R fluently, but produce
> tidyverse. When you must touch base (modeling internals, DESeq2, matrix
> math), isolate it in a small function with a tidy wrapper.
> :::

All `{webr}` cells on a page **share one R session**, and all `{pyodide}`
cells share one Python session — `library()` / `import` once and every later
cell can use them.

## Pattern 1 — Vectorization

No `for` loop: operate on the whole vector at once. This is R's single most
important idea — it exists because R's interpreter is slow per-element but
its C-level vector ops are fast, and because statistics *thinks* in columns.

```{webr}
#| label: p1-r
x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)

x * 2 + 1                    # every element, at once
ifelse(x > 4, "hi", "lo")    # vectorized if — returns a vector
sqrt(x)                      # every math function is vectorized
pmax(x, 5)                   # element-wise max against a scalar
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: p1-py
# Python: plain lists can't do this... numpy can
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])

print(x * 2 + 1)
print(np.where(x > 4, "hi", "lo"))
print(np.sqrt(x))
print(np.maximum(x, 5))
```

Why not loop? Three reasons: **speed** (C vs interpreter), **clarity** (the
intent is "transform all of it"), and **safety** (no index bookkeeping, no
off-by-one). A row-wise `for` loop over a data frame is almost always a
vectorized one-liner in disguise.

::: {.callout-tip}
## R vs Python indexing heads-up
R vectors are **1-indexed**; numpy arrays are **0-indexed**. Full table in
[Day 2](day2-data-structures.qmd).
:::

## Pattern 2 — The pipe (data first)

```{webr}
#| label: p2-r
library(dplyr)

mtcars |>
  filter(cyl != 4) |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(mean_mpg = mean(mpg))
```

Read it as a sentence: *"take mtcars, **then** filter, **then** group, **then**
summarise."* The pipe works because every dplyr verb takes the data frame as
its **first argument** — the pipe inserts the left side into the first
argument slot of the right side.

The alternative without pipes shows why they won:

```r
# same thing, upside-down reading order + naming tax
by_cyl <- group_by(filter(mtcars, cyl != 4), cyl)
result <- summarise(by_cyl, mean_mpg = mean(mpg))
rm(by_cyl)
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: p2-py
# Python: the same "sentence" is method chaining
import pandas as pd

# small mtcars subset (in-browser cells avoid big downloads)
mtcars = pd.DataFrame({
    "mpg": [21.0, 21.0, 22.8, 18.7, 14.3, 24.4,
            19.2, 17.3, 33.9, 21.5, 13.3, 32.4],
    "cyl": [6, 6, 4, 8, 8, 4, 6, 8, 4, 4, 8, 4],
})

(mtcars
   .query("cyl != 4")
   .groupby("cyl")["mpg"]
   .mean())
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## AI-code smell
`mtcars2 <- filter(mtcars, ...)`, `mtcars3 <- group_by(mtcars2, ...)`,
`df_final <- summarise(mtcars3, ...)` — pipe-less tidyverse with a naming tax
for every step. Refactor into one `|>` chain. The intermediate names carry
zero information and invite reusing the wrong one.
:::

## Pattern 3 — df-in, df-out functions

```{webr}
#| label: p3-r
library(dplyr)

summarise_cyl <- function(df, min_mpg = 0) {
  df |>
    filter(mpg >= min_mpg) |>
    group_by(cyl) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean_mpg = mean(mpg))
}

summarise_cyl(mtcars, min_mpg = 15)
```

The shape is always: **data in → pipeline → data out**. One function = one
verb-sized transformation. This is what makes analyses *composable* — you
stack three small functions instead of copy-pasting five lines into a new
script (and forgetting one).

Two small habits that make Pattern 3 professional-grade:

```r
# 1. name data arguments `df` (or `data`) so readers know where the pipe enters
# 2. give defaults so the function has a sensible zero-argument behavior
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: p3-py
def summarise_cyl(df, min_mpg=0):
    return (df[df["mpg"] >= min_mpg]
              .groupby("cyl")["mpg"]
              .agg(["count", "mean"])
              .reset_index())

summarise_cyl(mtcars, min_mpg=15)
```

## Pattern 4 — The formula interface

The tilde is R's mini-language for "left side explained by right side."

```{webr}
#| label: p4-r
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
summary(fit)$coefficients
```

You will meet formulas everywhere: `lm`, `glm`, `boxplot(mpg ~ cyl)`,
aggregate, lattice, mixed models, and — critically for you — **DESeq2
designs** (`design = ~ batch + condition`) and edgeR model matrices.
**Formulas are the single most reused syntax in applied R statistics.**

Two reading rules:
- `~` separates response (left) from predictors (right); nothing on the left
  (`~ x + y`) is still a formula — just a structure spec (how DESeq2 uses it)
- `+` inside a formula means "and also this term", **not** arithmetic

```{pyodide}
#| label: p4-py
# Python borrowed the exact idea (patsy formula language)
# NOTE: first run downloads statsmodels — takes ~30s once, then it's cached
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

df = mtcars.assign(wt=[2.62, 2.875, 2.32, 3.44, 3.57, 3.19,
                       3.92, 3.73, 1.835, 2.465, 3.84, 2.2])
fit = smf.ols("mpg ~ wt + C(cyl)", data=df).fit()
print(fit.params)
```

Note the tiny dialect difference: R wraps a raw column with `factor(cyl)`,
patsy uses `C(cyl)`. Same concept: "treat as categorical."

## Pattern 5 — Tidy eval: `{{ }}` (recognize, don't memorize)

When a function takes a *column name* as an argument, dplyr needs `{{ }}`
to look inside it:

```{webr}
#| label: p5-r
library(dplyr)

group_mean <- function(df, group_col, value_col) {
  df |>
    group_by({{ group_col }}) |>
    summarise(mean = mean({{ value_col }}))
}

group_mean(mtcars, cyl, mpg)
```

Why does this exist? dplyr verbs capture what you *type* (`cyl` the symbol,
not the string `"cyl"`) so they can both find the column and label output
correctly. Inside your own function you re-capture with `{{ }}`. You mostly
need to **recognize** it so wrappers in AI-generated code stop looking alien.

## Pattern 6 — Functionals (loops in disguise)

```{webr}
#| label: p6-r
library(purrr)

genes <- list(A = c(3, 5, 8), B = c(1, 9), C = c(4, 4, 4, 4))

map_dbl(genes, mean)          # named double vector of means
map_int(genes, length)        # named integer vector of lengths
map(genes, \(g) g / sum(g))   # any function, list out
```

The purrr suffix is the return type: `map_dbl` → doubles, `map_int` →
integers, `map_chr` → strings, plain `map` → list. That type discipline is
exactly what `sapply()` lacks (it guesses — and guesses wrong at length 1,
a classic silent bug).

Rule of thumb: `map()` for transformation, `walk()` for side-effects
(plots, saves), `map_dfr()`/`list_rbind()` for "read many files, bind into
one table".

```{pyodide}
#| label: p6-py
genes = {"A": [3, 5, 8], "B": [1, 9], "C": [4, 4, 4, 4]}

print({k: sum(v) / len(v) for k, v in genes.items()})   # comprehension = map
print({k: len(v) for k, v in genes.items()})
print({k: [x / sum(v) for x in v] for k, v in genes.items()})
```

## Pattern 7 — S3 dispatch (why `summary()` is psychic)

`summary()`, `plot()`, `print()` behave differently depending on the **class**
of the object. That's S3: one generic function, many per-class methods,
chosen at call time by looking at `class(x)`.

```{webr}
#| label: p7-r
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
class(fit)                          # "lm"
length(methods(plot))               # dozens of plot.<class> methods
```

When you read AI-generated R that calls `plot(res)` and wonder "what does
plot do here?" — the answer is always in the class. Discover the whole API
of any object with `methods(class = "...")`.

```python
# Python: the same concept is dunder methods + classes (conceptual)
# print(obj)  calls obj.__str__
# len(obj)    calls obj.__len__
# df.head()   is a method on the DataFrame class
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## This pays off in bioinformatics
`DESeqDataSet`, `Seurat` objects, `SingleCellExperiment`, `phyloseq` — all
are S3/S4 objects. When `plot(x)` "just works" on them, you now know why,
and you know how to enumerate what else you can call on them.
:::

## Read & refactor: AI code in the wild

Real pattern: chatbot-generated R that *works* but teaches you nothing.
Diagnose it with the 7 patterns:

```r
# ❌ Before: valid R, zero patterns
result <- c()
for (i in 1:length(mtcars$cyl)) {
  if (mtcars$cyl[i] > 4) {
    result[i] <- mtcars$mpg[i] * 1.1
  } else {
    result[i] <- mtcars$mpg[i]
  }
}
mtcars$mpg_adj <- result
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The diagnosis
1. `1:length(...)` is a **real bug** — if the vector is empty this becomes
   `1:0` = `c(1, 0)` and the loop still runs, writing garbage. Use `seq_along()`.
2. Row-wise loop + `if` = Pattern 1 (`if_else`) begging to be used.
3. Growing a vector with `result <- c(result, ...)`-style assignments is
   O(n²) and fragile.
4. Direct `df$col[i]` indexing is base dialect; data should flow through a pipe.
:::

```{webr}
#| label: refactor-good
# ✅ After: Pattern 1 + Pattern 2, one line of intent
mtcars_adj <- mtcars |>
  mutate(mpg_adj = if_else(cyl > 4, mpg * 1.1, mpg))

head(mtcars_adj, 3)
```

One more — recognize before you scroll:

```r
out <- lapply(split(df, df$batch), function(d) {
  coef(lm(y ~ x, data = d))
})
do.call(rbind, out)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The patterns inside
`split` + `lapply` + `do.call(rbind, ...)` is the base-R ancestor of
`group_by() |> group_modify() |> ...` (Patterns 2+3) and of purrr's
`map() |> list_rbind()` (Pattern 6). You don't have to *write* this style,
but half the StackOverflow answers for R are written in it.
:::

## Drills (live pad)

Predict each output **before** running. Easy → spicy, top to bottom.

```{webr}
#| label: drills
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

# 1. Convert c(15, 22, 9, 30) °C to °F  (F = C * 9/5 + 32)

# 2. Label mtcars$cyl "low" (== 4) / "high" (otherwise) — one call

# 3. Top 3 rows of mtcars by hp, descending — one pipe

# 4. Mean of each column of mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")] — one functional

# 5. boxplot of mpg split by am — formula style

# 6. How many rows have mpg above the MEDIAN mpg? (chain, no intermediate)

# 7. map over c(2, 4, 8) producing each value cubed, as a double vector

# 8. Add column z = mpg / wt; keep rows where z > 8; return wt and z

# 9. group_mean(mtcars, am, hp) — write group_mean with {{ }} first

# 10. From the p6 `genes` list: total length of all elements combined

# 11. data.frame of cyl → number of rows, via summarise — but sorted

# 12. In one pipe: for each carb value, the max hp; label the column top_hp
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `c(15, 22, 9, 30) * 9 / 5 + 32`
2. `if_else(mtcars$cyl == 4, "low", "high")`
3. `mtcars |> arrange(desc(hp)) |> slice_head(n = 3)`
4. `map_dbl(mtcars[, c("mpg", "hp", "wt")], mean)`
5. `boxplot(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars)`
6. `mtcars |> filter(mpg > median(mpg)) |> nrow()` — 15
7. `map_dbl(c(2, 4, 8), \(v) v^3)`
8. `mtcars |> mutate(z = mpg / wt) |> filter(z > 8) |> select(wt, z)`
9. see Pattern 5 cell — `group_by({{ group_col }}) |> summarise(mean = mean({{ value_col }}))`
10. `reduce(map_int(genes, length), `+`)` — or `sum(unlist(genes))`
11. `mtcars |> count(cyl) |> arrange(desc(n))`
12. `mtcars |> group_by(carb) |> summarise(top_hp = max(hp))`
:::

## Python drills (live pad)

Same reflexes, other dialect. All numpy/pandas — predict first.

```{pyodide}
#| label: drills-py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 1. Convert [15, 22, 9, 30] °C to °F

# 2. Label cyl == 4 "low" / otherwise "high" for the mtcars subset

# 3. Top 3 rows of mtcars by mpg, descending

# 4. Mean of each column of mtcars

# 5. Mean mpg per cyl count, sorted ascending by mean

# 6. Rows where mpg is above the median mpg — how many?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers (Python)
1. `np.array([15, 22, 9, 30]) * 9 / 5 + 32`
2. `np.where(mtcars["cyl"] == 4, "low", "high")`
3. `mtcars.sort_values("mpg", ascending=False).head(3)`
4. `mtcars.mean(numeric_only=True)`
5. `mtcars.groupby("cyl")["mpg"].mean().sort_values()`
6. `(mtcars[mtcars["mpg"] > mtcars["mpg"].median()])` then `len(...)` — 5
   (median = 21.0, and ties don't count)
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — vectorize the loop

Rewrite `classify_gc()` **without** any loop or `if`, using vectorization.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d1-vector
classify_gc <- function(gc_scores, threshold = 50) {
  # Return "high" or "low" for every score, vectorized
  # (gc_scores is like c(39.2, 55.1, 48.7, 61.0))
  ______
}

classify_gc(c(39.2, 55.1, 48.7, 61.0))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-vector"}
`if_else(condition, "high", "low")` or `ifelse()` — one call, whole vector.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-vector"}
```r
classify_gc <- function(gc_scores, threshold = 50) {
  if_else(gc_scores > threshold, "high", "low")
}
```
:::

### Exercise 1b — same, in Python

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d1-vector-py
import numpy as np

def classify_gc(gc_scores, threshold=50):
    ______

print(classify_gc(np.array([39.2, 55.1, 48.7, 61.0])))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-vector-py"}
`np.where(gc_scores > threshold, "high", "low")`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-vector-py"}
```python
import numpy as np

def classify_gc(gc_scores, threshold=50):
    return np.where(gc_scores > threshold, "high", "low")
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — build a pipe

Using `mtcars`: keep rows with `wt > 2`, then for each `cyl` compute
`n` and `mean_wt`, sorted by `mean_wt` descending. One pipe.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d1-pipe
library(dplyr)

heavy_summary <- mtcars |>
  ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-pipe"}
Verbs in order: `filter()` → `group_by()` → `summarise(n = n(), mean_wt = mean(wt))` → `arrange(desc(mean_wt))`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-pipe"}
```r

  filter(wt > 2) |>

```

Write `peak_table(df, group_col, value_col)` that returns one row per group
with `n`, `mean`, `max` of the value column. It must work for ANY grouping
column — test with `cyl` and with `gear`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d1-fn
library(dplyr)

peak_table <- function(df, group_col, value_col) {
  ______
}

peak_table(mtcars, cyl, hp)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-fn"}
Start the pipe with `df |> group_by({{ group_col }})` and summarise all
three statistics from `{{ value_col }}`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-fn"}
```r
peak_table <- function(df, group_col, value_col) {
  df |>
    group_by({{ group_col }}) |>
    summarise(
      n    = n(),
      mean = mean({{ value_col }}),
      max  = max({{ value_col }})
    )
}
```
:::

### Exercise 4 — refactor the crime scene

Refactor this into idiomatic tidyverse (hint: it's TWO problems in one):

```r
tmp <- data
for (i in 1:nrow(tmp)) {
  if (tmp$expr[i] < 1) {
    tmp$level[i] <- "silent"
  } else if (tmp$expr[i] < 10) {
    tmp$level[i] <- "low"
  } else {
    tmp$level[i] <- "high"
  }
}
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d1-refactor
library(dplyr)
data <- tibble::tibble(expr = c(0.3, 4.2, 33.0, 9.9))

# your refactored version:
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d1-refactor"}
One `mutate()` with `case_when(expr < 1 ~ "silent", expr < 10 ~ "low", .default = "high")`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d1-refactor"}
```r
data <- data |>
  mutate(level = case_when(
    expr < 1  ~ "silent",
    expr < 10 ~ "low",
    .default  = "high"
  ))
```
:::

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. `1:length(x)` — the shapeshifting bug
`length(0)` is 0, so `1:0` is `c(1, 0)` — a loop that runs *twice* on
nothing. `seq_along(x)` returns an empty vector when `x` is empty. This bug
ships in AI-generated R constantly.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. `ifelse()` vs `if_else()`
Base `ifelse()` silently drops attributes (dates become numbers!) and
recycles uneven vectors without complaint. `dplyr::if_else()` checks types
and lengths. Default to `if_else()`/`case_when()`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. Growing vectors in loops
`out <- c(out, new)` inside a loop copies the whole vector every iteration
(O(n²)). Collect into a `list()` and combine once — or don't loop at all.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
# Q1: what prints?
x <- c(3, 1, 2)
x[c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)]

# Q2: what prints?
mtcars |> group_by(cyl) |> summarise(n = n()) |> nrow()

# Q3: what prints?
map_int(c("a", "abc", ""), nchar)

# Q4: what is different?
f <- function(df, col) df[[col]]
f(mtcars, "mpg") |> class()

# Q5: what prints, and why is it spooky?
y <- c()
length(1:length(y))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. `3 2` — logical index keeps positions 1 and 3
2. `3` — three distinct cylinder counts (4, 6, 8)
3. `1 3 0` — nchar per string, as integers
4. `numeric`/`double` — `df[[col]]` returns the *contents* (a vector),
   whereas `df[col]` would return a one-column data frame
5. `2` — `1:length(y)` is `1:0` = `c(1, 0)`, length 2. This is pitfall #1.
:::

- [ ] I write `|>` chains instead of `df2`, `df3`, `df_final`
- [ ] Formula syntax no longer looks like magic
- [ ] I scored 5/5 on the self-quiz (or at least learned why I didn't)
